message.content:
Yes to both.

**Retries**: a delivery that returns non-2xx or takes >10s retries on an exponential schedule — 1m, 5m, 30m, 2h, 8h — then is dropped. Each attempt shows in the dashboard [webhooks-retries].

**Idempotency**: dedupe on `X-Meridian-Delivery-Id`, which stays stable across retries of the same event [webhooks-headers] — or on `event.id` in the payload if you'd rather key on the event itself [events-schema]. Store processed ids and skip repeats.

One caveat worth designing for: ordering across *different* events is not guaranteed, so idempotency alone isn't enough if your handler assumes sequence [webhooks-ordering].

messages.content: Explain to a non-technical exec why we can't just 'add more servers' to fix our database being slow. One paragraph, no jargon.

message.content: Adding servers helps when the problem is too many customers waiting in line — you open more checkout lanes. But our database is slow for a different reason: it's like one filing cabinet that every lane has to walk back to for every order. Adding lanes doesn't speed up the cabinet; it actually makes the crowd around it worse. The real fixes are making fewer trips to the cabinet (smarter queries), keeping copies of the most-used files at each lane (caching), or reorganizing the cabinet so lookups are faster (indexing). Those are engineering changes, not purchasing decisions — cheaper than servers, but they take focused time from the team.

messages.content: I have chicken thighs, a lemon, feta, orzo, and a sad-looking zucchini. 30 minutes. What do I make?

message.content:
One-pan lemon chicken orzo — perfect for exactly that inventory.

1. **Sear** (8 min): Salt the thighs, sear skin-side down in an oven-safe pan until deep golden. Flip, 2 min, remove. Don't wash the pan — that fond is the flavor.
2. **Toast** (2 min): Half-moon the zucchini, brown it in the chicken fat, then stir in the orzo (about 1 cup) for 30 seconds.
3. **Simmer** (12 min): Add 2 cups of water or stock, juice of half the lemon, scrape the bottom. Nestle the thighs back on top, lid on, medium-low until the orzo is tender.
4. **Finish**: Off heat — crumble feta over, zest the lemon on top, squeeze the rest of the juice, black pepper.

The orzo drinks the chicken juices and the feta half-melts into a sauce. The sad zucchini will not be recognized.

message.content:
Easy on both counts:

- **No stock**: water works fine here — the seared-chicken fond plus the rendered fat basically makes stock in the pan. Add an extra pinch of salt and, if you have it, a knob of butter with the water.

Everything else — timing, order, the feta finish — stays exactly the same.

messages.content: Do webhook deliveries retry, and can I make them idempotent on my side?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[webhooks-retries] Failed deliveries (non-2xx or >10s timeout) retry on an exponential schedule: 1m, 5m, 30m, 2h, 8h, then dropped. Each attempt is logged in the dashboard.
[webhooks-headers] Every delivery includes `X-Meridian-Delivery-Id` (stable across retries of the same event) and `X-Meridian-Signature`.
[webhooks-ordering] Delivery order is not guaranteed across events; consumers must not assume sequence.
[events-schema] Event payloads carry `event.id`, unique per event.

function.name: search_docs
function.description: Semantic search over the product documentation corpus.

message.content:
Yes to both.

**Retries**: a delivery that returns non-2xx or takes >10s retries on an exponential schedule — 1m, 5m, 30m, 2h, 8h — then is dropped. Each attempt shows in the dashboard [webhooks-retries].

**Idempotency**: dedupe on `X-Meridian-Delivery-Id`, which stays stable across retries of the same event [webhooks-headers] — or on `event.id` in the payload if you'd rather key on the event itself [events-schema]. Store processed ids and skip repeats.

One caveat worth designing for: ordering across *different* events is not guaranteed, so idempotency alone isn't enough if your handler assumes sequence [webhooks-ordering].

message.content:
It's **flat** — p95 sits at 1.84-1.94s whether the query returns 0 results or 500. A regression proportional to result size would slope upward; this doesn't.

That rules out serialization/payload cost and points at fixed per-request overhead added on Aug 4: most likely the reranker model call that deploy enabled, or a lost index forcing a full scan even for empty results (an empty-result full scan still reads the whole table). I'd check `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` on a zero-hit query first — if it's the index, that's a one-line fix.

messages.content: Explain to a non-technical exec why we can't just 'add more servers' to fix our database being slow. One paragraph, no jargon.

message.content: Adding servers helps when the problem is too many customers waiting in line — you open more checkout lanes. But our database is slow for a different reason: it's like one filing cabinet that every lane has to walk back to for every order. Adding lanes doesn't speed up the cabinet; it actually makes the crowd around it worse. The real fixes are making fewer trips to the cabinet (smarter queries), keeping copies of the most-used files at each lane (caching), or reorganizing the cabinet so lookups are faster (indexing). Those are engineering changes, not purchasing decisions — cheaper than servers, but they take focused time from the team.

messages.content: I have chicken thighs, a lemon, feta, orzo, and a sad-looking zucchini. 30 minutes. What do I make?

message.content:
One-pan lemon chicken orzo — perfect for exactly that inventory.

1. **Sear** (8 min): Salt the thighs, sear skin-side down in an oven-safe pan until deep golden. Flip, 2 min, remove. Don't wash the pan — that fond is the flavor.
2. **Toast** (2 min): Half-moon the zucchini, brown it in the chicken fat, then stir in the orzo (about 1 cup) for 30 seconds.
3. **Simmer** (12 min): Add 2 cups of water or stock, juice of half the lemon, scrape the bottom. Nestle the thighs back on top, lid on, medium-low until the orzo is tender.
4. **Finish**: Off heat — crumble feta over, zest the lemon on top, squeeze the rest of the juice, black pepper.

The orzo drinks the chicken juices and the feta half-melts into a sauce. The sad zucchini will not be recognized.

No stock, and my partner hates zucchini skin. Adjust?

message.content:
Easy on both counts:

- **No stock**: water works fine here — the seared-chicken fond plus the rendered fat basically makes stock in the pan. Add an extra pinch of salt and, if you have it, a knob of butter with the water.
- **Zucchini skin**: peel it before slicing (a Y-peeler takes 20 seconds), and cut slightly thicker half-moons so the peeled flesh doesn't go mushy. Browning them well in step 2 also builds enough texture that the skin won't be missed.

Everything else — timing, order, the feta finish — stays exactly the same.

message.content:

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[webhooks-retries] Failed deliveries (non-2xx or >10s timeout) retry on an exponential schedule: 1m, 5m, 30m, 2h, 8h, then dropped. Each attempt is logged in the dashboard.
[webhooks-headers] Every delivery includes `X-Meridian-Delivery-Id` (stable across retries of the same event) and `X-Meridian-Signature`.
[webhooks-ordering] Delivery order is not guaranteed across events; consumers must not assume sequence.

function.name: search_docs
function.description: Semantic search over the product documentation corpus.

message.content:
Yes to both.

**Retries**: a delivery that returns non-2xx or takes >10s retries on an exponential schedule — 1m, 5m, 30m, 2h, 8h — then is dropped. Each attempt shows in the dashboard [webhooks-retries].

**Idempotency**: dedupe on `X-Meridian-Delivery-Id`, which stays stable across retries of the same event [webhooks-headers] — or on `event.id` in the payload if you'd rather key on the event itself [events-schema]. Store processed ids and skip repeats.

One caveat worth designing for: ordering across *different* events is not guaranteed, so idempotency alone isn't enough if your handler assumes sequence [webhooks-ordering].

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[auth-rotation] Rotating a key creates a new secret immediately; the previous secret remains valid for 24 hours by default (configurable 0-72h via `grace_period_hours`).

function.name: search_docs
function.description: Semantic search over the product documentation corpus.

message.content:
There's a grace period for **rotation**, not for revocation:

- **Rotate**: the new secret works immediately and the old one keeps working for 24 hours by default — tunable from 0 to 72 hours with `grace_period_hours` [auth-rotation]. So a rolling deploy can swap secrets with zero downtime.
- **Revoke**: immediate invalidation. Requests already authenticated and in flight complete; new ones fail [auth-revoke].

Both actions land in the audit log within a minute if you need to verify [auth-audit].

messages.content: I have chicken thighs, a lemon, feta, orzo, and a sad-looking zucchini. 30 minutes. What do I make?

message.content:
One-pan lemon chicken orzo — perfect for exactly that inventory.

1. **Sear** (8 min): Salt the thighs, sear skin-side down in an oven-safe pan until deep golden. Flip, 2 min, remove. Don't wash the pan — that fond is the flavor.
2. **Toast** (2 min): Half-moon the zucchini, brown it in the chicken fat, then stir in the orzo (about 1 cup) for 30 seconds.
3. **Simmer** (12 min): Add 2 cups of water or stock, juice of half the lemon, scrape the bottom. Nestle the thighs back on top, lid on, medium-low until the orzo is tender.
4. **Finish**: Off heat — crumble feta over, zest the lemon on top, squeeze the rest of the juice, black pepper.

The orzo drinks the chicken juices and the feta half-melts into a sauce. The sad zucchini will not be recognized.

No stock, and my partner hates zucchini skin. Adjust?

message.content:
Easy on both counts:

- **No stock**: water works fine here — the seared-chicken fond plus the rendered fat basically makes stock in the pan. Add an extra pinch of salt and, if you have it, a knob of butter with the water.
- **Zucchini skin**: peel it before slicing (a Y-peeler takes 20 seconds), and cut slightly thicker half-moons so the peeled flesh doesn't go mushy. Browning them well in step 2 also builds enough texture that the skin won't be missed.

Everything else — timing, order, the feta finish — stays exactly the same.

  SELECT date_trunc('month', trial_started_at) AS signup_month,

message.content:
Yes to both.

**Retries**: a delivery that returns non-2xx or takes >10s retries on an exponential schedule — 1m, 5m, 30m, 2h, 8h — then is dropped. Each attempt shows in the dashboard [webhooks-retries].

**Idempotency**: dedupe on `X-Meridian-Delivery-Id`, which stays stable across retries of the same event [webhooks-headers] — or on `event.id` in the payload if you'd rather key on the event itself [events-schema]. Store processed ids and skip repeats.

One caveat worth designing for: ordering across *different* events is not guaranteed, so idempotency alone isn't enough if your handler assumes sequence [webhooks-ordering].

messages.content: What happens to in-flight requests when I rotate an API key? Is there a grace period?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[auth-rotation] Rotating a key creates a new secret immediately; the previous secret remains valid for 24 hours by default (configurable 0-72h via `grace_period_hours`).
[auth-revoke] Revoking (as opposed to rotating) invalidates the secret immediately; in-flight requests already authenticated are allowed to complete.
[auth-audit] Key events (created, rotated, revoked, expired) appear in the audit log within 60 seconds.

function.name: search_docs
function.description: Semantic search over the product documentation corpus.

message.content:
There's a grace period for **rotation**, not for revocation:

- **Rotate**: the new secret works immediately and the old one keeps working for 24 hours by default — tunable from 0 to 72 hours with `grace_period_hours` [auth-rotation]. So a rolling deploy can swap secrets with zero downtime.
- **Revoke**: immediate invalidation. Requests already authenticated and in flight complete; new ones fail [auth-revoke].

Both actions land in the audit log within a minute if you need to verify [auth-audit].

messages.content: I have chicken thighs, a lemon, feta, orzo, and a sad-looking zucchini. 30 minutes. What do I make?

request.system: You are a helpful assistant.

messages.content: I have chicken thighs, a lemon, feta, orzo, and a sad-looking zucchini. 30 minutes. What do I make?

message.content:
One-pan lemon chicken orzo — perfect for exactly that inventory.

1. **Sear** (8 min): Salt the thighs, sear skin-side down in an oven-safe pan until deep golden. Flip, 2 min, remove. Don't wash the pan — that fond is the flavor.
2. **Toast** (2 min): Half-moon the zucchini, brown it in the chicken fat, then stir in the orzo (about 1 cup) for 30 seconds.
3. **Simmer** (12 min): Add 2 cups of water or stock, juice of half the lemon, scrape the bottom. Nestle the thighs back on top, lid on, medium-low until the orzo is tender.
4. **Finish**: Off heat — crumble feta over, zest the lemon on top, squeeze the rest of the juice, black pepper.

The orzo drinks the chicken juices and the feta half-melts into a sauce. The sad zucchini will not be recognized.

No stock, and my partner hates zucchini skin. Adjust?

message.content:
Easy on both counts:

- **No stock**: water works fine here — the seared-chicken fond plus the rendered fat basically makes stock in the pan. Add an extra pinch of salt and, if you have it, a knob of butter with the water.
- **Zucchini skin**: peel it before slicing (a Y-peeler takes 20 seconds), and cut slightly thicker half-moons so the peeled flesh doesn't go mushy. Browning them well in step 2 also builds enough texture that the skin won't be missed.

Everything else — timing, order, the feta finish — stays exactly the same.

messages.content: Do webhook deliveries retry, and can I make them idempotent on my side?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[webhooks-retries] Failed deliveries (non-2xx or >10s timeout) retry on an exponential schedule: 1m, 5m, 30m, 2h, 8h, then dropped. Each attempt is logged in the dashboard.
[webhooks-headers] Every delivery includes `X-Meridian-Delivery-Id` (stable across retries of the same event) and `X-Meridian-Signature`.
[webhooks-ordering] Delivery order is not guaranteed across events; consumers must not assume sequence.
[events-schema] Event payloads carry `event.id`, unique per event.

function.name: search_docs
function.description: Semantic search over the product documentation corpus.

message.content:
Yes to both.

**Retries**: a delivery that returns non-2xx or takes >10s retries on an exponential schedule — 1m, 5m, 30m, 2h, 8h — then is dropped. Each attempt shows in the dashboard [webhooks-retries].

**Idempotency**: dedupe on `X-Meridian-Delivery-Id`, which stays stable across retries of the same event [webhooks-headers] — or on `event.id` in the payload if you'd rather key on the event itself [events-schema]. Store processed ids and skip repeats.

One caveat worth designing for: ordering across *different* events is not guaranteed, so idempotency alone isn't enough if your handler assumes sequence [webhooks-ordering].

message.content:
Yes to both.

**Retries**: a delivery that returns non-2xx or takes >10s retries on an exponential schedule — 1m, 5m, 30m, 2h, 8h — then is dropped. Each attempt shows in the dashboard [webhooks-retries].

**Idempotency**: dedupe on `X-Meridian-Delivery-Id`, which stays stable across retries of the same event [webhooks-headers] — or on `event.id` in the payload if you'd rather key on the event itself [events-schema]. Store processed ids and skip repeats.

One caveat worth designing for: ordering across *different* events is not guaranteed, so idempotency alone isn't enough if your handler assumes sequence [webhooks-ordering].

messages.content: What happens to in-flight requests when I rotate an API key? Is there a grace period?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[auth-rotation] Rotating a key creates a new secret immediately; the previous secret remains valid for 24 hours by default (configurable 0-72h via `grace_period_hours`).
[auth-revoke] Revoking (as opposed to rotating) invalidates the secret immediately; in-flight requests already authenticated are allowed to complete.
[auth-audit] Key events (created, rotated, revoked, expired) appear in the audit log within 60 seconds.

- **Rotate**: the new secret works immediately and the old one keeps working for 24 hours by default — tunable from 0 to 72 hours with `grace_period_hours` [auth-rotation]. So a rolling deploy can swap secrets with zero downtime.

messages.content: What happens to in-flight requests when I rotate an API key? Is there a grace period?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[auth-rotation] Rotating a key creates a new secret immediately; the previous secret remains valid for 24 hours by default (configurable 0-72h via `grace_period_hours`).
[auth-revoke] Revoking (as opposed to rotating) invalidates the secret immediately; in-flight requests already authenticated are allowed to complete.
[auth-audit] Key events (created, rotated, revoked, expired) appear in the audit log within 60 seconds.

function.name: search_docs
function.description: Semantic search over the product documentation corpus.

message.content:
There's a grace period for **rotation**, not for revocation:

- **Rotate**: the new secret works immediately and the old one keeps working for 24 hours by default — tunable from 0 to 72 hours with `grace_period_hours` [auth-rotation]. So a rolling deploy can swap secrets with zero downtime.
- **Revoke**: immediate invalidation. Requests already authenticated and in flight complete; new ones fail [auth-revoke].

Both actions land in the audit log within a minute if you need to verify [auth-audit].

message.content:
Two great rooftop-pool options under $300:

1. **Memmo Príncipe Real — $289/night** ($1,156 for 4 nights). 9.3 rating, breakfast included, and the rooftop looks over the whole city down to the river. Príncipe Real is the best neighborhood in Lisbon for a relaxed trip: 10 minutes' walk to Chiado, surrounded by the good restaurants.
2. **EPIC SANA Marquês — $244/night** ($976). Bigger, more polished-corporate, proper heated rooftop pool.

With the TAP flights, Memmo puts the trip at **$2,452** — still under $2,500. That's the one I'd book. Shall I hold it?

messages.content: What happens to in-flight requests when I rotate an API key? Is there a grace period?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[auth-rotation] Rotating a key creates a new secret immediately; the previous secret remains valid for 24 hours by default (configurable 0-72h via `grace_period_hours`).
[auth-revoke] Revoking (as opposed to rotating) invalidates the secret immediately; in-flight requests already authenticated are allowed to complete.
[auth-audit] Key events (created, rotated, revoked, expired) appear in the audit log within 60 seconds.

function.name: search_docs
function.description: Semantic search over the product documentation corpus.

message.content:
There's a grace period for **rotation**, not for revocation:

- **Rotate**: the new secret works immediately and the old one keeps working for 24 hours by default — tunable from 0 to 72 hours with `grace_period_hours` [auth-rotation]. So a rolling deploy can swap secrets with zero downtime.
- **Revoke**: immediate invalidation. Requests already authenticated and in flight complete; new ones fail [auth-revoke].

Both actions land in the audit log within a minute if you need to verify [auth-audit].

message.content:
Two great rooftop-pool options under $300:

1. **Memmo Príncipe Real — $289/night** ($1,156 for 4 nights). 9.3 rating, breakfast included, and the rooftop looks over the whole city down to the river. Príncipe Real is the best neighborhood in Lisbon for a relaxed trip: 10 minutes' walk to Chiado, surrounded by the good restaurants.
2. **EPIC SANA Marquês — $244/night** ($976). Bigger, more polished-corporate, proper heated rooftop pool.

With the TAP flights, Memmo puts the trip at **$2,452** — still under $2,500. That's the one I'd book. Shall I hold it?

Thanks,
Sam

messages.content: Do webhook deliveries retry, and can I make them idempotent on my side?

messages.name: search_docs
messages.content:
[webhooks-retries] Failed deliveries (non-2xx or >10s timeout) retry on an exponential schedule: 1m, 5m, 30m, 2h, 8h, then dropped. Each attempt is logged in the dashboard.
[webhooks-headers] Every delivery includes `X-Meridian-Delivery-Id` (stable across retries of the same event) and `X-Meridian-Signature`.
[webhooks-ordering] Delivery order is not guaranteed across events; consumers must not assume sequence.
[events-schema] Event payloads carry `event.id`, unique per event.

function.name: search_docs
function.description: Semantic search over the product documentation corpus.

message.content:
Yes to both.

**Retries**: a delivery that returns non-2xx or takes >10s retries on an exponential schedule — 1m, 5m, 30m, 2h, 8h — then is dropped. Each attempt shows in the dashboard [webhooks-retries].

**Idempotency**: dedupe on `X-Meridian-Delivery-Id`, which stays stable across retries of the same event [webhooks-headers] — or on `event.id` in the payload if you'd rather key on the event itself [events-schema]. Store processed ids and skip repeats.

One caveat worth designing for: ordering across *different* events is not guaranteed, so idempotency alone isn't enough if your handler assumes sequence [webhooks-ordering].

message.content:
Two great rooftop-pool options under $300:

1. **Memmo Príncipe Real — $289/night** ($1,156 for 4 nights). 9.3 rating, breakfast included, and the rooftop looks over the whole city down to the river. Príncipe Real is the best neighborhood in Lisbon for a relaxed trip: 10 minutes' walk to Chiado, surrounded by the good restaurants.
2. **EPIC SANA Marquês — $244/night** ($976). Bigger, more polished-corporate, proper heated rooftop pool.

With the TAP flights, Memmo puts the trip at **$2,452** — still under $2,500. That's the one I'd book. Shall I hold it?
